{{nihongo|'''Ogawatsuki Shrine'''|小川月神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tanba Province]].

=== Enshrined deities ===
* '''{{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|qid=Q595520|qid=Q595520|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto}}''' (つくよみのみこと)

Along the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōi River}}, there are other shrines of the {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|Q710302|qid=Q710302}} lineage, so a connection with {{ill|Tsukiyomi Shrine (Kyoto)|Q11516217|qid=Q11516217|lt=Kuzuno-ni-masu Tsukiyomi Shrine}} (a {{ill|Sessha|Q135009904|qid=Q135009904}} of Matsuo Taisha) downstream has been noted<ref>'Nihon no Kamigami,' Ogawatsuki Shrine entry.</ref>.

=== About the shrine name ===
The shrine name is considered to have been formed by prefixing the district name "Ogawa-gō" to the shrine name.

The shrine is located on the left bank (east side) of the Ōi River, but across the river to the west, in Chiyokawa-chō, there is a place name Ogawa, which is considered to be the surviving place name of "Ogawa-gō, Kuwata District" appearing in '{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Wamyō Ruijushō}}.' Therefore, it is thought that the old course of the Ōi River ran east of the shrine, and the shrine area was formerly included in Ogawa-gō. The Furukawa River flowing east of the shrine is considered a remnant of the Ōi River's course change<ref>'Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Place Names of Kyoto Prefecture' ({{ill|Heibonsha|Q11482108|qid=Q11482108}}), Ogawatsuki Shrine entry.</ref>.

Before the Meiji era, the shrine was called "Tsukiyomi(-jin)ja," and even today it is affectionately known as "Tsukiyomi-san."

=== History ===
=== General history ===
Given the connection with Matsuo Taisha mentioned above, it is thought that the {{ill|Hata clan|Q987290|qid=Q987290}} advanced upstream along the Ōi River in the course of their development, and the shrine was founded in connection with that process. A document of unknown date preserved by the parishioner representatives, titled "On Ogawatsuki Shrine, Kuwata District, Tanba Province," states either that the shrine was a {{ill|Massha|ja|末社|qid=Q135009906}} when {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|qid=Q687168|lt=the two Ise shrines}} were temporarily relocated to {{ill|Tango Province|Q1054331|qid=Q1054331}} {{ill|Yosa District, Kyoto|Q1078639|qid=Q1078639}}, or that it was a massha while located in {{ill|Tanba Province|cs|Tanba (provincie)|de|Provinz Tamba|es|Provincia de Tanba|fa|ولایت تانبا|fr|Province de Tanba|gl|Provincia de Tanba|id|Provinsi Tamba|it|Tanba (provincia)|ja|丹波国|ko|단바국|lt|Tambos žemė|nl|Tamba (provincie)|pt|Província de Tanba|ru|Тамба (провинция)|simple|Tamba Province|sk|Tanba (provincia)|sr|Провинција Тамба|tr|Tamba (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тамба|zh|丹波國|zh_min_nan|Tanba-kok|qid=Q954511}}, describing the site as "an ancient place since the age of the gods." It further states that the shrine is older than Izumo Shrine (the present {{ill|Izumo-daijingū|Q10896675|qid=Q10896675}} in Kameoka, Chitose-chō), equal in status to that shrine, and "the second great shrine" of {{ill|Kuwada district|ja|桑田郡|zh|桑田郡|qid=Q11537600}}.

According to the 'Shrine Registry,' during the {{ill|Ōnin|Q1143903|qid=Q1143903|lt=Ōnin era}} (1467-69), a flood of the Ōi River washed away the shrine grounds, and thereafter the shrine was maintained as a small subsidiary shrine. The aforementioned document also records a flood during the {{ill|Ōei|Q1193078|qid=Q1193078|lt=Ōei era}} (1394-1428), and alternatively states that it fell into disrepair due to warfare, after which "the precinct became narrow and there were no rituals." From these accounts, it is thought that the shrine was damaged by the Ōi River's course change and other events, and fell into decline.

On the opposite bank of the Ōi River, in Chiyokawa-chō Ogawa, there is also a Tsukiyomi Shrine enshrining Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto. This is thought to have been ritually invited from Ogawatsuki Shrine by people who became separated from it due to the Ōi River's course change, and established as their new tutelary shrine. The bridge over the Ōi River connecting Kameoka's Maji-chō and Chiyokawa-chō was named "Tsukiyomi Bridge" by local politician Tsutsumi Tasakichi, because shrines dedicated to Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto stand on both banks.

In the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} era, the shrine was ranked as a village shrine, but in Meiji 10 ({{ill|1877|Q7773|qid=Q7773}}), it was identified as the Engishiki-listed Myōjin Taisha, and a confirmation document issued by Kyoto Prefecture in June of that year states: "Tsukiyomi-sha: confirmed to be the Engishiki-listed Ogawatsuki Shrine."

=== Shrine rank ===
* {{ill|Ten'an|Q1075611|qid=Q1075611|lt=Ten'an}} 3 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}), January 27: promoted from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade ('{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}') - recorded as "Ogawa Tsukushin."

=== Shrine priests ===
The aforementioned parishioner representative document states: "Since Sadamura took charge of guardianship, spring and autumn rituals have been held without interruption." According to shrine tradition, {{ill|Hōjō Tokiyori|Q1354410|qid=Q1354410}}, while traveling the country, visited the shrine and ordered his retainer Hitomi Jirō Sadamura to serve as its guardian. The Hitomi family served for 30 generations, but subsequently the parishioner representatives took over the shrine's maintenance and management (from the precinct information board).

=== Precinct ===
The precinct stands amid paddy fields south of {{ill|Nantan High School|Q11375232|qid=Q11375232|lt=Nantan High School}}. Since the 1.3-hectare area of paddy land centered on the shrine bears the place name "Tsukiyomi," it is speculated that this paddy land was once the shrine's sacred domain.

The honden is a one-bay {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|fr|Nagare-zukuri|it|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|pl|Nagare-zukuri|ru|Нагарэ-дзукури|sv|Nagare-zukuri|zh|流造|qid=Q210684}} structure standing within a shelter building. The haiden is a one-bay, gable-entry, tile-roofed structure, said to have been relocated from Izumo Daijingū at an unknown date. The precinct has been selected by Kameoka City as one of "Kameoka's 100 Natural Treasures" under the name "Ogawatsuki Shrine."

=== Main festivals ===
At the annual festival on {{ill|October 16|Q2963|qid=Q2963}}, there is a custom of offering prayers for all children born during the year. Although the origin of this custom is unknown, the entire community comes together to pray for the healthy growth of its children.
